description: Needed skills: Ideas, graphic design, UIUX, creativity
summary: Save the Rabbit is a story-driven browser game about designing space missions the way NASA does. Luna, a rabbit geologist, is stranded at the Moon's south pole, and the player, a young rocket builder, has six missions to bring her home, from a first rocket flight to the final rescue. Every mission follows NASA's steps: need and goals, concept of operations, requirements with a planned verification method, design, build and verify, then fly. Players choose parts under a budget, and a deterministic physics simulation flies their design; the animation and graphs are drawn from that same calculation. When a design fails, the debrief names the first cause in plain language and suggests what to change, so failure becomes the lesson. After three missions, a Challenges map opens with eight harder solo puzzles that add real launch rules: max-Q, booster landing, fairing heating, g-limits, debris disposal and mass margin. The game turns systems-engineering thinking (trade-offs, requirements and verification) into play for teenagers and adults, with no account or download needed.
details:
Save the Rabbit is a browser game about planning space missions. Luna, a rabbit geologist, is stuck at the Moon's south pole, and you're the rocket builder who has to bring her home. You work up to it over six missions. First a small rocket that only has to reach 30 km, then a satellite in orbit, a radio relay around the Moon, a survey of landing sites, a cargo landing, and finally the rescue itself.

Each mission is planned by starting with why the mission exists and who is involved. Then you get a short list of requirements, each with a note on how you'll prove you met it. After that you pick parts, stay under budget, and press Test. A physics simulation flies your design, and the animation you watch is drawn from those same numbers. If the rocket falls short, the game tells you what went wrong first ("the engine is too weak for how heavy the rocket is") and suggests what to change. Then you try again. That loop of building, testing and fixing is the heart of the game.

After three missions, a Challenges map opens: eight harder puzzles, drawn as little turning planets. Some add rules real launch teams deal with, like how much air pressure the rocket can survive, landing the booster back at the launch site, and not leaving the upper stage behind as space junk. The last one is very hard on purpose.

We wanted a game about the thinking engineers actually do, not just flying or memorizing facts. Every choice costs something, a requirement only counts if you can check it, and a failed test tells you something. We hope teenagers and adults come away understanding why missions are designed the way they are, and maybe thinking "I could do that too."

Creativity-wise, we iterated frequently on the game's look and feel, including the color themes, art style, motion design, sound effects and more, to build an immersive experience for players. The whole goal is to "save the rabbit": rescue Luna, who is stranded on the Moon, through a series of space missions, which adds a layer of story to plain mission building. We also intentionally added humor to the story, like Luna's obsession with rocks.

Coding-wise, the project was build with TypeScript and React (using Vite), with canvas and SVG graphics and sound made in the browser with the Web Audio API. The simulations are our own code and always give the same result for the same design, so scores are fair. Automated tests check the physics and play the whole campaign from start to finish. It runs in any modern browser on a computer or phone, with no download or account, and your progress is saved in your own browser.

The mission steps are based on NASA's "Design and Develop Science Missions" webinar and the NASA Systems Engineering Handbook (SP-2016-6105). The physics is simplified and the part values are made up for simplicity of the gameplay. The game lists every simplification in its top right info page. The character and scene art is AI-generated pixel art and the music was made with Suno; we directed both and chose the results. We used Claude Code, an AI coding assistant, to help implement technical changes.
